title: SDG Digital Acceleration Agenda: Leveraging Digital Technologies to Accelerate Progress Toward the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals
location: The principal location where the event/document originates is Geneva, Switzerland. This is because the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), one of the lead organizations of the SDG Digital Acceleration Agenda, is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, and the document is a joint publication by ITU and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), both UN entities with strong presence in Geneva.
executive_summary: The SDG Digital Acceleration Agenda, launched by ITU and UNDP in 2023, highlights the transformative potential of digital technologies to accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). With 2.6 billion people still offline, the agenda emphasizes inclusive digital transformation, focusing on digital skills, governance, infrastructure, financing, and security. It showcases 34 proven digital solutions across all 17 SDGs, demonstrating how technologies like mobile money, AI, IoT, and digital public infrastructure can improve health, education, financial inclusion, climate action, and governance. The agenda stresses the need for whole-of-government and whole-of-society approaches, collaboration among stakeholders, and robust protections to mitigate risks such as digital divides, cybersecurity threats, and bias. Emerging technologies, if responsibly deployed, can further amplify impact. To realize this potential, strategic leadership, sustainable financing, and inclusive policies are essential. The agenda calls for scaling proven solutions, enhancing partnerships, and investing in digital ecosystems to ensure no one is left behind in the digital future.
characteristics: The SDG Digital Acceleration Agenda, launched by ITU and UNDP in 2023, aims to leverage digital technologies to accelerate progress on the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), addressing areas like digital skills, governance, infrastructure, financing, and security.

Digital technologies can play three key roles for the SDGs: as channels for vital services, sources of data and insights, and catalysts for broader progress, directly benefiting about 70% of SDG targets.

The Agenda showcases 34 diverse digital solutions aligned with each SDG, emphasizing inclusive, people-centered design, collaboration, scalability, and appropriate technology use to ensure positive impact.

Digital transformation requires a whole-of-society approach involving governments, private sector, and civil society, supported by key enablers such as national digital vision, digital public infrastructure, connectivity, data governance, digital skills, and financing models.

Emerging technologies like AI, IoT, blockchain, and 5G have the potential to amplify SDG progress but also pose risks including bias, cybersecurity threats, and digital divides, necessitating inclusive governance and safeguards.

The Agenda stresses the urgency of inclusive digital transformation to bridge digital divides (gender, urban-rural), build digital literacy, ensure cybersecurity, and foster multi-stakeholder collaboration to realize the full potential of digital for sustainable development.

practical_applications: ITU and UNDP have launched the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Digital Acceleration Agenda to drive universal and meaningful connectivity and digital transformation aligned with the SDGs.
Implementation of 34 proven digital solutions across all 17 SDGs, including:
M-Pesa (mobile money service) for financial inclusion in Kenya, Egypt, Ghana, Lesotho, Mozambique, and Tanzania.
GiveDirectly (mobile cash transfer) in Uganda, Togo, DRC, Liberia, Malawi, Mozambique, Nigeria, Rwanda, Bangladesh.
DHIS2 (health-care management system) in Haiti, Honduras, Uganda, Sri Lanka, The Gambia.
OpenIMIS (open-source social protection management software) in Bangladesh, Cameroon, Chad, DRC, Gambia, Mauritania, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Nepal, Tanzania, Zambia.
Atingi (online learning platform) in Zimbabwe, Egypt, Mexico, Costa Rica, Sudan, Poland.
UNICEF Learning Passport (mobile online/offline learning platform) in 34 countries.
Audiopedia (audio education app for women with low literacy) in multiple countries including Pakistan, India, Nigeria, Uganda.
USAID/Microsoft Airband Initiative (addressing gender digital divide) in Guatemala, Ghana, India, Colombia, Kenya.
Gybe (water system monitoring via satellite and sensors) in multiple countries including Viet Nam, Kenya, US, Brazil.
CityTaps (smart prepaid water meters) in Niger, Burkina Faso, Senegal, Kenya, Namibia, Ecuador, Singapore.
Nithio (AI-enabled financing for off-grid solar) in Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda.
COMET (electricity demand assessment for mini-grids) in Malaysia, Indonesia, Myanmar, Somaliland, India, Nepal, Fiji.
Giga (school connectivity initiative by ITU and UNICEF) connecting over 5,000 schools in 20+ countries.
Smart Facilities for Health (digitally-enabled health infrastructure) in Guinea-Bissau, India, Indonesia, Sao Tome and Principe, South Sudan, Uganda.
Mobile Innovation Hub (accelerator for local digital innovation ecosystems) in Tunisia, Indonesia.
SkillLab (AI-driven skills mapping and job matching) in Jordan, Iraq, Lebanon, Finland, Mexico, US.
Balady (national smart city platform) in Saudi Arabia.
HOT Tasking Manager (volunteer mapping tool) active globally.
OpenSC (supply-chain transparency platform) in DRC, Guatemala, Colombia, India, Australia.
Winnow Vision (AI food waste management) in UK, US, UAE, Japan, Germany, Mexico, Ireland, Norway, Netherlands.
WIPO GREEN (online platform for green technology exchange) active in multiple countries.
IMEO (International Methane Emissions Observatory) providing methane emissions data globally.
CounterMEASURE (plastic pollution reduction in rivers) in Thailand, Sri Lanka, India.
Connected Mangroves (mangrove forest monitoring) in Malaysia, India, Philippines.
Rainforest Connection (AI acoustic monitoring to halt illegal logging) in Peru, Brazil, Tanzania, Indonesia, Poland, Costa Rica, Ecuador.
UN Biodiversity Lab (mapping and analytics for biodiversity) in 140+ countries.
Digital Family Card (government e-services platform) in Kazakhstan.
MigApp (migration services app) used globally.
Partner2Connect (multistakeholder alliance to foster connectivity) active in Dominican Republic, Madagascar.
Data4SDGs (global data partnership network) active in 40+ countries.
Mizan II (case management system for judiciary) in Palestine.
eyeWitness to Atrocities app (evidence collection for justice) in Nigeria, Gambia, Senegal, Palestine, DRC, Ukraine.
National digital transformation examples:
Singapore’s Smart Nation initiative with 99% government services digitalized and strong leadership.
Rwanda’s digital literacy increase from 8% to 35% adult digital literacy through coordinated policies and #ConnectRwanda initiative.
Bangladesh’s a2i program embedding SDGs into digital public services, saving citizens over USD 20 billion.
Argentina Conectada’s Refefo fibre-optic network connecting 1,129 locations, improving internet quality and affordability.
China’s rural digital access expansion through broadband plans and subsidies, increasing rural internet penetration to 62%.
Philippines telecom tower sector reform reducing permit approval from 241 to 16 days, expanding free internet to thousands of isolated areas.
India’s Aadhaar biometric digital ID program covering over 90% of population, saving government USD 10 billion.
Estonia’s X-Road open-source data exchange platform enabling 99% of public services online, saving government 2% GDP.
Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) development including digital IDs, payments, data sharing, digital signatures, and open APIs to enable scalable, interoperable digital ecosystems.
Multistakeholder collaborations such as the Digital Public Goods Alliance, Partner2Connect, and Data4SDGs to foster partnerships, resource mobilization, and data sharing.

Financing mechanisms including blended finance, public-private partnerships, digital connectivity infrastructure funds, and credit-enhancement facilities to mobilize investments for digital transformation.
Capacity building initiatives for digital skills, digital literacy, and AI-enabled job matching (e.g., SkillLab).
Cybersecurity capacity building through National Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRT) and international standards.
Inclusive digital transformation approaches prioritizing marginalized groups, gender equality, and human rights protections.
Annual AI for Good Global Summit hosted by ITU and partners to scale AI solutions for SDGs and address governance and ethical challenges.
Youth engagement platforms like UNICEF U-Report active in 60+ countries to amplify youth voices in digital and SDG agendas.

kpi_list.kpi_text: Mobilize at least USD 3.7 to 4.2 trillion annually to fill the SDG funding gap by 2030
kpi_list.target_description: Close the annual funding gap required to achieve the SDGs
kpi_list.measurement_method: Tracking annual funding mobilization against SDG financing needs
kpi_list.responsible_entity: National governments, multilateral development banks, private sector, donors

kpi_list.kpi_text: Connect every school – and ultimately every community – in the world to the Internet by 2030
kpi_list.target_description: Achieve universal Internet connectivity for schools and communities worldwide
kpi_list.measurement_method: Percentage of schools with Internet access reported by national education and ICT authorities

kpi_list.kpi_text: Ensure 70 per cent of SDG targets directly benefit from digital technologies by 2030
kpi_list.metric_name: SDG Targets Benefiting from Digital Technologies
kpi_list.target_description: Proportion of SDG targets accelerated or supported by digital technologies
kpi_list.measurement_method: Analysis of SDG targets and digital technology impact mapping
kpi_list.responsible_entity: UN agencies, national governments, digital development partners

kpi_list.kpi_text: Reduce the gender digital divide where women are 17 per cent less likely to own a smartphone compared to men in low- and middle-income countries
kpi_list.target_description: Eliminate the smartphone ownership gap between women and men
kpi_list.measurement_method: Surveys and data collection on smartphone ownership by gender
kpi_list.responsible_entity: National governments, private sector, civil society

kpi_list.kpi_text: Increase adult digital literacy in Rwanda from 8 per cent in 2017 to approximately 35 per cent by 2023
kpi_list.target_description: Proportion of adults able to access online services independently
kpi_list.measurement_method: National digital literacy surveys and assessments

kpi_list.kpi_text: Establish a strong, ambitious, and credible national digital transformation vision aligned with development goals
kpi_list.target_description: Develop and adopt a comprehensive digital vision grounded in population needs and aligned with SDGs
kpi_list.measurement_method: Existence and implementation of national digital strategy documents and frameworks

kpi_list.kpi_text: Build interoperable Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) including digital IDs, payments, data sharing, and consent mechanisms
kpi_list.target_description: Develop and implement interoperable DPI components to enable public and private service delivery at scale
kpi_list.measurement_method: Assessment of DPI components deployed and their interoperability and usage

kpi_list.kpi_text: Scale proven digital solutions such as Digital Public Goods (DPGs) that demonstrate measurable impact and replicability
kpi_list.target_description: Adopt and scale digital solutions with demonstrated impact and sustainability across countries
kpi_list.measurement_method: Number of countries adopting and scaling proven digital solutions; impact evaluations
kpi_list.responsible_entity: National governments, UN agencies, private sector, civil society

kpi_list.kpi_text: Strengthen cybersecurity capacity and governance to protect digital infrastructure and users
kpi_list.target_description: Enhance national cybersecurity frameworks, incident response teams, and public awareness to mitigate cyber risks
kpi_list.measurement_method: Cybersecurity Index scores, existence of national CERTs/CIRTs, cybersecurity policies and enforcement

kpi_list.kpi_text: Foster multistakeholder collaboration among governments, private sector, civil society, and international partners for inclusive digital transformation
kpi_list.target_description: Establish and maintain partnerships and collaborative platforms to align efforts and resources for digital transformation
kpi_list.measurement_method: Number and effectiveness of multistakeholder initiatives, partnerships, and alliances
kpi_list.responsible_entity: National governments, UN agencies, private sector, civil society

top_actors.name: International Telecommunication Union (ITU)
top_actors.justification: ITU is a lead organization prominently mentioned throughout the document as a key driver of the SDG Digital Acceleration Agenda. It plays a central role in digital infrastructure, connectivity, governance, and global coordination efforts, and is involved in multiple initiatives and partnerships critical to the agenda.

top_actors.name: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
top_actors.justification: UNDP is co-lead with ITU and deeply involved in shaping, supporting, and implementing the digital acceleration agenda. It provides strategic leadership, policy frameworks, and operational support, and is frequently cited in relation to digital transformation, inclusion, and SDG progress.

top_actors.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
top_actors.justification: IDB is a key knowledge partner and supporter, contributing expertise on financing, innovation, and regional digital transformation, especially in Latin America and the Caribbean. It is involved in initiatives like fAIr LAC and financing models, making it influential in the economic and implementation aspects of the agenda.

top_themes.name: Digital Acceleration (Digital Transformation & Strategy)
top_themes.justification: This theme is the core focus of the entire document, framing the agenda around accelerating digital transformation to achieve the SDGs. It encompasses strategy, vision, and holistic approaches that guide all other themes, making it central to the document's main message and strategic importance.

top_themes.name: Digital Infrastructure (Digital Transformation & Strategy)
top_themes.justification: Digital infrastructure is foundational to enabling digital acceleration and transformation. The document dedicates significant content to connectivity, digital public infrastructure, and technical enablers, highlighting their critical role in achieving universal and meaningful connectivity and supporting digital solutions at scale.

top_themes.name: Digital Inclusion (Inclusion & Social Development)
top_themes.justification: Ensuring that digital transformation benefits everyone, especially marginalized groups, is a recurring and strategic priority throughout the document. The agenda emphasizes closing digital divides (gender, rural-urban, skills), embedding protections, and fostering inclusive digital skills development, which are essential to fulfilling the SDGs equitably.
